entities.name: Venus of Savignano
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Venus of Savignano, dating to approximately 22,000 BCE, is a remarkable prehistoric sculpture discovered in the Italian region of Emilia-Romagna. This figurine exemplifies the artistic expression of the Upper Paleolithic period, marking a significant point in human cultural development, as it reflects the complex social and symbolic lives of early humans. Its discovery near the Savignano sul Panaro area underscores the artistic endeavors of prehistoric societies, showcasing the importance of female figures in early art as representations of fertility and femininity.

Carved from limestone, the Venus of Savignano stands at about 15 centimeters tall, characterized by exaggerated features that symbolize the human form in a stylized manner. It was unearthed during archaeological excavations that aimed to explore the rich prehistoric heritage of Italy. The sculpture is part of a broader category of Venus figurines that have been found across Europe, illustrating a shared cultural motif among hunter-gatherer societies of the time, where such figures likely held ritualistic or symbolic significance related to fertility, survival, and the human condition.

The legacy of the Venus of Savignano extends beyond its artistic value; it has influenced contemporary understandings of prehistoric art and the role of women in ancient societies. This figurine contributes to the discourse on gender representations in early cultures, prompting further research into the social structures of prehistoric communities. The interest it generates among archaeologists and historians continues to inspire debates about the meanings and functions of prehistoric art within the broader framework of human history.
